name: Beth Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, so please give me what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What is an ordinary day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior developer at a tech company that makes fare software for city buses. I fix small bugs in transfers and refunds, then ask a senior developer to check my work. I have a two-year college diploma and I'm still learning the tricky fare rules. A rider once showed us two charges for one journey, and I liked being able to make the next bill right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home and with nearby work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a nurse with regular hours, and we have children aged nine and twelve and a mortgage. This tech company pays me well for a junior, and we have around eight months of expenses saved. Plenty of other software teams are nearby, although they may not pay the same. I use AI now and then, after somebody tests it on a real fare case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team a small code helper can draft routine refund tests if a person still checks the fare rule. A rider should not have to argue with an automated double charge. We already know how to review those cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my job and my partner's nursing wage to hold. Eight months saved means a normal bad month would not threaten the mortgage. I would still watch whether the helper creates more refund work than it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing the fare bugs with senior review and try the helper only on old refund cases once our team checks it. We'd continue our existing transfer from each payday to the emergency account. In the first year I'd record any wrong fare the helper misses before asking for wider use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I have a wage, a buffer and nearby employers. A little automation doesn't change the shape of our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fare case would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A child changed buses within the free transfer period and was charged twice. I'd use that old case first, with customer details removed. The tool has to catch the second charge, not just write a neat test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a rider waiting for a refund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a person will check the journey record and give a date for the correction. The rider should not have to become a software tester to get their money back. I'd put that rule in the release notes.

say: I'd use a **small helper** only on checked refund tests with human fare-rule review.
I'd insist a **double-charged rider** has a person to contact.
think: I expect my **developer wage** and my partner's nursing pay to continue.
Our **eight-month buffer** protects the mortgage from an ordinary setback.
do: Keep **fixing fare bugs** with a senior developer checking releases.
Continue **payday savings transfers** and record wrong fares before expanding helper use.
feel: **Calm** about household work and money under modest change.
S0.quote: The rider should not have to become a software tester to get their money back.
fieldNote: She links AI trial results to a **child's double charge**, not abstract productivity claims.
Higher junior pay, nursing income and **eight months saved** support calm about current bills.
The existing savings transfer is **new pay saved**, not a relabeling of reserve cash.

steps.text: Keep correcting fare software with senior review before releases
Continue transferring new pay into emergency savings each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers that AI taking code, checks and customer replies will hit junior jobs first. I'd ask our staff association to count vacant posts that go unfilled and demand paid training time. I'd also ask riders to report wrong refunds during a trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose the well-paid junior place before I've become a strong developer. Another nearby firm might hire me, but I can't assume it would match this wage. Eight months saved gives us choices, not the right to ignore a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I'd attend the association meeting and ask for a written headcount plan. I'd learn the new AI refund-check tool on old cases during paid work time if a senior reviewer signs off each result. If my hours fall in the first year, we'd cancel the planned new sofa and I'd apply to nearby transit-software teams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can ask for facts and learn a tested tool, but the word 'junior' is right there in my contract. I don't want a warm speech in place of a pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should join the trial meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invite the bus drivers who hear complaints before our developers do. A driver knows when a rider paid twice. Our staff association should hear that before claiming the software is ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really learn the new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the senior reviewer shows me where it failed on old cases and I get paid time. I use AI sometimes already; this would be a new refund-check workflow. I won't practice on live rider accounts first.

say: I'd ask our **staff association** to count unfilled posts and secure paid training.
I'd include **bus drivers** in trials of automated refunds.
think: I could lose a **well-paid junior post** before my skills catch up.
I cannot assume a **nearby software firm** will match my present wage.
do: Attend the **association meeting** and request a written staffing plan next week.
Learn the **new refund-check workflow** on old cases during paid supervised time.
Cancel the **planned sofa** and apply nearby if my developer hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about losing higher junior pay despite savings and local alternatives.
S1.quote: I don't want a warm speech in place of a pay cheque.
fieldNote: She links workforce action to **unfilled junior posts**, reflecting her progressive outlook.
Her new AI learning is a **specific refund workflow** with paid time and senior review.
The sofa cancellation and applications depend on **reduced hours**, not a forecast alone.

steps.text: Attend staff association meeting and request a written headcount plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm full thinking AI by 2028 could do our code and refund checks before robots reach hands-on bus maintenance around 2031. I'd ask the association for written layoff dates and a human appeal for riders. I wouldn't say my partner's nursing work makes my wage disposable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer job could end. Eight months saved and a nursing wage would keep the mortgage paid for a while, but our children and house need more than one income over the years. A local coding vacancy might also disappear under the same cheap AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask for a work reference and put an extra amount from each pay cheque into the emergency account while both wages hold. I'd ask the transit office about paid fare-dispute roles and their actual wages. In the first year after 2028, if laid off, I'd apply for a paid transit-support opening only if one exists and its pay with nursing income covers mortgage and school costs; I'd ask about public retraining grants before paying for a course, and enroll only if funding covers the fee and pickup times fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make the calls, but I expect a large wage loss before the next school year feels settled. Eight months of savings are time to act, not a replacement career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask it to demand a written notice period and paid time for anyone moving into transit support. We have to know the dates before a family spends its buffer. I would attend the meeting, not just sign a note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What course would you consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A transit customer-service course might teach how appeals actually get settled. I would take a funded place only if a paid opening asks for that skill and the classes fit school pickup. A certificate without a vacancy won't pay the mortgage.

say: I'd demand **written layoff dates** and a human fare appeal as 2028 thinking AI arrives.
I'd explain that **2031 maintenance robots** follow the threat to our screen work.
think: I expect my **developer job** could end despite nearby software firms.
Our **eight-month buffer** and nursing wage buy time, not years of replacement income.
do: Save an **extra payday amount** while both wages hold and request a work reference.
Attend the **association meeting** for written notice and paid transition time.
Apply for **paid transit support** after layoff if wages cover family bills; enroll in required training only with funding and pickup fit.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss before a new paid role is secured.
S2.quote: Eight months of savings are time to act, not a replacement career.
fieldNote: Her partner’s **nursing wage** buys time while thinking AI threatens her junior coding pay by 2028.
She draws on **collective action** for notice and paid transition time while adding new pay to savings.
Transit work and study depend on **real paid openings**, family-bill coverage, funding and school pickup.

steps.text: Add new pay to emergency savings while both household wages hold
Attend staff association meeting to demand written notice and paid transition time
Apply for paid transit support if laid off and combined wages cover mortgage and school costs
Enroll in funded transit service course only if paid vacancies require it and classes fit pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our firm to publish yearly numbers for junior jobs and paid training places. Five years before 2031 is enough to teach riders' appeal work while we're still earning. Robots around 2034 may later affect maintenance, but our code changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a record of fare cases and learn customer appeals, though AI may answer those too. My partner and I can save more on two wages, but a paid transit job must exist before I switch. I don't want to gamble our eight-month reserve on a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd enroll in the transit office's appeal course if the company pays the fee and gives work time; if not, I'd self-fund only if paid vacancies require it and our eight months of essentials remain untouched. We'd add a fixed extra amount from each pay cheque toward a ten-month buffer if both wages keep coming. In the first year after 2031, if coding hours shrink and a paid appeal post exists, I'd apply before leaving the developer job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years lets me learn and save, but I still think a junior seat could vanish. I would read each staffing report, not file it away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practice on an appeal day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow a rider's double-charge complaint from the bus record to a corrected bill, with a supervisor watching. I'd ask why a person overturned the automatic answer. That is work I can learn, even if it may shrink later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if one wage falls before you reach ten months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the extra transfer before touching the mortgage payment. Eight months saved is the floor for paying bills while we look for work. The target is only a target, not a reason to miss a bill.

feel: **Anxious** about a junior cut, with time to build savings and appeal skills.
S3.quote: I don't want to gamble our eight-month reserve on a title.
fieldNote: Her next skill is grounded in **actual fare appeals**, not a claim that customer work is AGI-proof.
The ten-month target uses **new wages only**, with the existing eight-month reserve protected.
A move requires **shrinking coding hours** and a paid transit vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger developers to learn who gets hurt by a wrong fare, not just how to write a test. A decade before 2036 gives employers time to pay for that learning. Thinking AI still reaches code before hands-on robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be skilled enough for a different paid role by my early fifties. We have steady nursing income, eight months saved and other local firms, so the next few years feel secure. I would not promise that the new role lasts forever just because it involves people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep developing, keep the payday savings transfer and ask for one paid transit-office day a month if my manager agrees. I'd complete a fare-appeals course only if it is employer-funded or paid vacancies require it and fees come from new savings beyond eight months. In the first year after 2036, if developer hours shrink, I'd apply for paid appeal or transit-software work that covers the mortgage and school costs before giving notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, calm about the next few years. I can change direction without putting the children through a sudden move now. I still want the company to say plainly where junior jobs are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the children's plans now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They are in school and our mortgage is manageable. I'd ask what they want to learn, and we'd adjust only if real pay changes. I won't turn a decade-long forecast into a household emergency today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave the developer job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written paid offer that covers the mortgage and school costs, with a supervisor who will teach the appeal work. I'd rather stay employed than collect certificates without a vacancy. We can use our buffer for a real gap, not a hopeful leap.

say: I'd ask for **paid fare learning** and clear junior-job forecasts across the decade.
I'd explain **2036 thinking AI** reaches code before later hands-on robots.
think: I could move into **paid appeal work** by my early fifties if jobs exist.
Our nursing income and **eight-month buffer** make the next few years secure.
do: Keep **developer work** and payday savings while asking for paid transit-office days if agreed.
Complete a **fare course** only with employer funding or required vacancies and new savings beyond eight months.
Apply for paid **appeal or software** posts if coding hours shrink after 2036 and wages cover family bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about later job demand, while calm about current household security.
S4.quote: I won't turn a decade-long forecast into a household emergency today.
fieldNote: Current high pay, nursing wages and **eight months saved** explain her near-term security.
She still wants **junior job forecasts** and keeps course spending beyond the emergency floor.
A future move requires a **written paid offer** covering mortgage and school costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I expect junior code work to shrink before I can be paid for anything else, and eight months saved won't replace a career. A written notice period, funded fare-appeals training and real paid transit openings would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether riders get a voice before an automated refund goes live. A bus driver hears the complaint before our dashboard does. I want riders and drivers at the table, not just the vendor and our manager.

headlineQuote: A bus driver hears the complaint before our dashboard does.
portrait: Beth is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, maintaining city-bus fare software while still learning.
She earns **higher junior pay**, shares a mortgage and two school-age children with a nurse partner, and has eight months saved.
She uses AI **occasionally** after testing, and wants riders, drivers and staff represented in software decisions.
The **2028 shock** alarms her because her junior wage may disappear before a paid replacement arrives.
Longer timelines allow **funded appeals training** and new savings without risking the eight-month reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her junior wage before paid transit work or funded training is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded fare-appeals training and real paid transit openings would help her family.
